options: One thread executes Python bytecode at a time, in one process
One thread runs at a time across all processes
Each line of Python is atomic
why: It exists to make reference counting correct without a lock on every object.

options: No faster, and sometimes slower once you count the switching
Faster if you use more of them
why: The lock is held while computing. It is released around waiting.

options: Is the work waiting, or computing
why: Waiting means threads or async. Computing means processes.

options: A read, an add and a write, so a switch between any two loses an update
Safe if the value is small
why: The GIL guarantees one bytecode at a time, not one line at a time.

q: Relying on which operations happen to be atomic is
options: A bad idea: it is an implementation detail, and the reasoning is invisible on the page
why: An uncontended lock costs far less than the bug does.

q: `if k not in d: d[k] = v`
options: Is two operations with a window between them, where a second worker reaches the same conclusion
Is safe because `d[k] = v` is one bytecode
why: `setdefault` does both as one operation, and `defaultdict` does it with a factory.

q: Two locks taken in different orders by two workers
options: Deadlock, and the fix is a global order for acquiring them
Deadlock, and the fix is a timeout
Are safe if both are released
why: Neither function is wrong alone. The bug exists only in the combination.

q: Processes differ from threads in that
options: They have separate interpreters and separate locks, and share nothing
They are limited by the GIL
why: Which makes them genuinely parallel, and makes everything crossing between them a copy.

q: Passing a large dataset to a process pool
options: Costs pickling, copying and unpickling, which can exceed the work saved
why: Invisible in a small test and decisive in a real one.

q: An exception raised inside a worker
options: Is stored in its `Future` and re-raised when somebody calls `.result()`
why: `.done()` is true either way, so a pool nobody reads swallows every failure.

options: `map` gives results in input order; `as_completed` yields them as they finish
why: Choosing between them is a question about what the caller does with the results.

options: Cannot be killed; it has to check a signal between units of work
Is killed when the main thread exits
Can be interrupted with an exception
why: Stopping one at an arbitrary instruction would leave whatever it held in an unknown state.

why: Right for a background heartbeat, wrong for anything holding data.
